In [[discrete geometry]], a [[abstract polytope|polytope]] is '''projectively unique''' (or '''projectively stable''') if it has a unique [[convex polytope|convex realization]] up to [[projective transformation]]s.

The study of projectively unique polytopes was initiated by [[Geoffrey C. Shephard]], [[Micha Perles]], [[Peter McMullen]] and [[Branko Grünbaum]]. Later significant contributions are also due to [[Karim Adiprasito]] and [[Günter M. Ziegler]].

== Introduction ==

Two convex polytope <math>P,Q\subset\Bbb R^n</math> are ''combinatorially equivalent'' if they have the same number of faces with the same incidence relations between them. Formally this means that <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> have isomorphic [[face lattice]]s, or equivalently, isomorphic underlying [[abstract polytope]]s.
One also says that both <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are ''realizations'' of the face lattice (or abstract polytope).

[[File:Equivalence types 2.png|400px|thumb|Different realizations of the cube. From left to right: 1) the standard cube; 2) an affine transformation of the standard cube; 3) a projective transformation of the standard cube that is not an affine transformation; 4) a realization of the cube that is not a projective transformation of the standard cube.]]

Given a convex polytope <math>P\subset\Bbb R^n</math> many combinatorially equivalent polytopes can be generated through transformation of the ambient space, such as [[isometries]] or [[affine transformation]]s.
The largest class of transformations of Euclidean space that preserves coplanarity, and hence maps polytopes onto combinatorially equivalent polytopes, is the class of [[projective transformation]]s. 
A polytope <math>P</math> is '''projectively unique''' if all other realizations are obtained through projective transformations; or in other words, if <math>P</math> has a ''unique'' convex realization up to projective transformations.

For example, [[Simplex (geometry)|simplices]], such as [[triangle]]s and [[tetrahedron|tetrahedra]], are projectively unique. 
In contrast, the [[cube]] is not projectively unique, as it has realizations that are not projectively equivalent to the standard cube (see the figure).

== Known projectively unique polytopes ==

Projective transformations on <math>n</math>-dimensional Euclidean space can map any <math>n+2</math> points onto any other <math>n+2</math> points. Hence, any <math>n</math>-dimensional polytope with at most <math>n+2</math> vertices is projectively unique.
Being projectively unique is moreover closed under [[Dual polyhedron|polar duality]].
Since duality swaps vertices and facets, any <math>n</math>-dimensional polytope with at most <math>n+2</math> facets is projectively unique as well. This shows that, for example, the [[Cartesian product|product]] of two simplices is projectively unique (such as the [[3-3 duoprism|(3,3)-duoprism]]). 
In dimension up to three, these are the only polytopes that are projectively unique, but in dimensions <math>n\ge 4</math> there are examples with more than <math>n+2</math> vertices and facets.

=== Dimension two ===

The following is the complete list of projectively unique polytopes in dimension two:

* [[triangle]]
* [[quadrilateral|quadrangle]]

=== Dimension three ===

A [[polyhedron|3-polytope]] is projectively unique if and only if it has at most nine edges.<ref name="AZ15"/>
The following is therefore the complete list of projectively unique polytopes in dimension three:

* [[tetrahedron]]
* [[square pyramid]]
* [[triangular prism]]
* [[triangular bipyramid]]

=== Operations ===

McMullen showed that projectively unique polytopes are closed under the following operations:<ref name="McMullenThesis"/><ref name="McMullen76"/>

* The [[join (topology)|join]] <math>P\star Q</math> of two polytopes is projectively unique if and only if the <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are projectively unique.
<!--* If <math>(P_1,F_1)\oplus (P_2,F_2)</math> are projectively unique, then <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are projectively unique, and the group of projective symmetries of <math>P_i</math> that fixes all the vertices acts transitively on the interior of <math>F_i</math>.-->
* The [[vertex sum]] <math>(P,v)\oplus (Q,w)</math> of two projectively unique polytopes is projectively unique.
* If <math>P</math> is projectively unique and <math>v</math> is a vertex of <math>P</math> so that <math>P</math> is ''not'' a vertex sum with distinguished vertex <math>v</math>, then the [[subdirect sum]] <math>(P,v)\oplus\Delta_1</math> is projectively unique (this is also known as ''splitting'' the vertex <math>v</math>).

These operations are sufficient to generate Shephard's list of projectively unique 4-polytopes. 
But not all projectively unique polytopes can be generated using these operations, for example, Perles' non-rational polytope (see below).

=== Other examples ===

Perles & Shephard (1974) used [[Gale diagram]]s to construct many projectively unique polytopes and showed that their number increases at least exponentially with the dimension.<ref name="PerlesShephard"/> 
In general, one can start from a projectively unique point-line configuration, for example, obtained by encoding a polynomial with a single real zero. After doubling all points this can be interpreted as the Gale diagram of a projectively unique polytope.
Starting from a suitable configuration (for example, the [[Perles configuration]]) this can be used to construct projectively unique polytopes that have no realization with rational coordinates.<ref name="Grünbaum"/>

Faces of projectively unique polytopes need not be themselves projectively unique.
In 2013 Adiprasito & Padrol showed that every polytope with algebraic vertex coordinates appears as a face of a projectively unique polytope.<ref name="AdiprasitoPadrol"/>
This shows that projectively unique polytopes satisfy a form of [[Mnëv's universality theorem|universality]] and that no simple structure theory can be expected.

In 2015 Adiprasito & Ziegler constructed infinitely many distinct projectively unique polytopes in dimension 69.<ref name="AZ15"/>
There are only finitely many projectively unique polytopes in dimension two and three, and it is an open question whether this is also the case in dimension four.

== Linearly unique polytopes ==

A [[central symmetry|centrally symmetric]] polytope <math>P</math> is '''linearly unique''' (or '''linearly stable''') if it has a unique origin symmetric realization up to linear transformations.
The class of linear unique polytopes is also closed under polar duality.
Examples of linearly unique polytopes are [[hypercube|cubes]] and [[crosspolytope]]s in all dimensions, and more generally, all [[Hanner polytope]]s.
In 1969 [[Peter McMullen]] showed that every centrally symmetric [[0/1-polytope]] is linearly unique.<ref name="McMullen69"/>
In the same paper McMullen sketches an argument that this gives a complete characterization of linearly unique polytopes.
Later, David Assaf (1976) constructs a counterexample, showing that McMullen's argument must be incomplete.<ref name="Assaf76"/> 
The counterexample provided is a centrally symmetric 0/1-polytope whose dual cannot be realized as a 0/1-polytope.

== Generalizations ==

For each natural number <math>k\ge 1</math> there are polytopes with precisely <math>k</math> distinct convex realizations up to projective transformations.
One way to construct such polytopes is using [[Gale diagram]]s. 
One starts from a point-line configurations with precisely <math>k</math> distinct realizations (up to projective transformations).
After doubling all points one can interpret it as the Gale diagram of a convex polytope.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/477622/are-there-polytopes-with-precisely-two-realizations |website=MathOverflow |access-date=1 August 2025 |title=Are there polytopes with precisely two realizations?}}</ref>
